I am a 46-year-old woman, and I have farmed these 3.5 mu in Quzhou for twenty years. My household has seven people, and some of my family work off-farm, which brings in cash, but this little plot is what feeds us. I grow wheat in winter and maize in summer—everyone here does the wheat-maize rotation. I cannot afford to take risks. I follow what has worked for me and my neighbors.

For wheat, I will plant in early October. I use an improved variety like Jimai 22 or Liangxing 99—seeds I buy from the local supply shop. Before sowing, I run the rotary tiller to prepare the seedbed. I put down compound fertilizer as a basal dressing—about one 50-jin bag per mu—and then I sow. Wheat needs water, so I will irrigate four times: the winter irrigation to protect against frost, then again at green-up, at jointing, and at grain filling. I pump from my well, so I watch the electricity cost, but I know skipping irrigation costs more in lost yield. At jointing, I topdress with urea. I spray pesticides about four times total—herbicide once early, then insecticide and fungicide when I see problems or when the weather turns humid. I expect about 1,050 jin of wheat per mu if the weather is normal.

For maize, as soon as the wheat comes off the thresher in early June, I plant the summer maize. I always use hybrid seed—Denghai 605 or something similar from the shop. I do not till again; I plant directly into the wheat stubble because there is no time to waste in the summer season, and everyone around me does no-tillage for maize now. I apply compound fertilizer at planting, and if the rains are not good, I side-dress with urea when the plants are knee-high. I irrigate twice—once if it is dry after sowing, and once at the big trumpet stage when the crop is thirstiest. Maize gets about four pesticide sprays too: herbicide at the start, then insecticide for corn borer, and fungicide if it stays wet. I expect about 1,200 jin per mu from the maize. This is my plan. I have done it many times, and it feeds my family.
